title: Managing Analytical Data
subtitle: Separate reporting needs from operational workloads
summary: Analytical and operational data serve different purposes, formats, and query patterns. The Data Warehouse centralizes extracted and transformed data so analysts can run specialized queries without burdening operational stores, but its pipelines and schema work are expensive and can become stale or rigid. The Data Lake reverses that model: it loads data in natural form and transforms it when a use appears, reducing premature work while shifting discovery, quality, and transformation burden to consumers. The chapter introduces Data Mesh as a newer response to the limits of centralized analytical platforms. Its key architectural question is where ownership, preparation, governance, and query cost should live as operational data becomes distributed. A useful design separates analytical access from transactional paths and chooses centralization, deferred transformation, or domain ownership according to actual consumers and quality requirements.

concepts.title: Two data purposes
concepts.body: Operational systems optimize current transactions and updates; analytical systems optimize queries, aggregations, historical views, and prediction. Their schemas and workloads differ, so joining them directly can add expensive work or destabilize transactional performance. Architecture must decide how analytical data is copied, shaped, owned, and queried.
concepts.example: Order placement needs fast writes and current state. Planning needs years of orders grouped by region and product, with calculations that should not compete with checkout traffic.

concepts.title: Data warehouse
concepts.body: A warehouse extracts data from many sources, transforms it into a designed analytical schema, loads it centrally, and runs analysis there. Central governance and predictable queries are useful, but extraction pipelines, transformation cost, storage, and freshness create substantial operational and maintenance commitments.
concepts.example: Nightly order, inventory, and customer extracts are conformed into reporting dimensions so finance can run repeatable regional revenue queries.

concepts.title: Data lake
concepts.body: A lake keeps the centralized model and pipelines but changes transform-and-load to load-and-transform. Raw data is stored in its natural format and transformed when a consumer has a concrete need. This avoids work for analyses that never arrive, while making discovery, quality, schema interpretation, and repeated transformation someone’s responsibility.
concepts.example: Raw clickstream, order, and sensor files land first. A data scientist later creates a curated feature set for a forecasting experiment rather than requiring every field to be modeled upfront.

concepts.title: Data Mesh direction
concepts.body: Data Mesh appears as a response to the limits of centralized analytical approaches in distributed organizations. The relevant trade-off shifts toward domain ownership, analytical data as a product, federated governance, and self-service capabilities. It distributes responsibility as well as data, so organizational readiness becomes part of the design.
concepts.example: Sales owns a documented revenue dataset while logistics owns delivery events; shared governance defines discoverability and quality expectations without one team transforming everything.

misconceptions.claim: A warehouse and operational database should always be the same store for simplicity.
misconceptions.correction: Analytical aggregation and historical queries can compete with transactional workloads and need different schemas. Separation is a workload trade-off, not needless duplication.

misconceptions.claim: A data lake removes data modeling and quality work.
misconceptions.correction: It defers transformation and makes raw data available; consumers still pay for interpretation, quality, lineage, and repeatable curated outputs.

scenario.title: Build planning analytics
scenario.context: An online retailer wants predictive inventory planning while checkout must remain reliable. Data comes from orders, warehouses, suppliers, and customer behavior. Analysts need reproducible metrics; data scientists need raw history; domain teams vary in their ability to document datasets. Choose an analytical arrangement and define where quality and ownership sit.

options.label: Warehouse first
options.benefit: Curated schemas and centralized governance support consistent reporting and protected operational workloads.
options.cost: Upfront extraction and transformation are expensive, and new exploratory uses wait for pipeline work.
options.consequence: Finance gets trusted weekly metrics quickly, but a new forecasting feature requires another modeled pipeline and may lag behind changing source data.

options.label: Lake with domains
options.benefit: Raw history supports exploration and domain teams can publish curated datasets as needs emerge.
options.cost: Consumers face discovery and quality variation, while governance and ownership require organizational discipline.
options.consequence: Data science starts from raw events, while inventory publishes a documented feature dataset. Shared checks are needed to prevent opaque, duplicated transformations.

scenario.debrief: Predictable recurring metrics favor curated warehouse paths; exploratory and distributed ownership needs favor lake or mesh practices. The decision must name who pays for freshness, quality, and transformation.

quiz.question: Why separate analytical and operational data?
options: Their workloads, schemas, and query purposes differ
quiz.explanation: Analytical aggregation can be costly and shaped differently from transactional updates.

quiz.question: What changes in a data lake?
options: Load natural data and transform when needed
quiz.explanation: The lake defers transformation; it does not eliminate the work or responsibility.

quiz.question: What organizational issue does a data mesh make explicit?
options: A requirement for one central schema
quiz.explanation: Mesh approaches distribute data product responsibility and require shared governance.

exercise.title: Trace an analytical product
exercise.prompt: Pick one analytical question. Map its operational sources, transformation point, owner, freshness expectation, quality checks, and consumer access path.

steps.text: Keep transactional records optimized for operational behavior.
Extract or load records into an analytical path with defined freshness.
Transform, document, and govern a reusable analytical dataset.
Run reporting or modeling without competing with checkout workloads.
